claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings is governed by dislocation transmission at heterointerfaces.
Severe lattice distortion and chemical short-range order cause interfaces produced under standard processing to be semi-coherent.
Baseline semi-coherent interfaces permit early dislocation crossing.
Early dislocation crossing at baseline interfaces produces localized plasticity.
Modified deposition parameters or a thin interlayer can produce more coherent and chemically uniform FCC/BCC interfaces.
Increasing interface coherency increases the barrier to dislocation transmission.
Increasing interface coherency promotes dislocation pile-up.
Increasing interface coherency delays dislocation transmission.
Delayed dislocation transmission leads to a more distributed and uniform pattern of plastic deformation.
Engineered coherent interfaces will reduce the steady-state creep rate relative to the semi-coherent baseline.
Engineered coherent interfaces will increase apparent strength under sustained loading relative to the baseline.
Engineered coherent interfaces will produce a more uniform distribution of plastic deformation than the baseline.
The baseline is a physical-vapor-deposited nanoscale multilayer of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers with semi-coherent interfaces.
The baseline interfaces exhibit pronounced lattice distortion and chemical short-range order.
The hypothesis is limited to multilayers whose individual layers remain in the tens-of-nanometers range.
The hypothesis is limited to temperatures below the onset of significant interdiffusion or phase transformation.
Failure of the higher-coherency multilayers to show both a significantly reduced steady-state creep rate and more uniform deformation relative to the baseline would reject the hypothesis.
